item.title: Why the same heat kills more in some places
item.description: A heat wave is counted twice: by thermometers, and by the registers of deaths. Plans work on the gap between the two.

item.title: Who keeps the clock?
item.description: Most governments now agree the twice-yearly clock change has outlived its use. They disagree on which hour to keep.

item.title: Does migration move voters to the right?
item.description: Studies that follow where newcomers actually settled find an effect, but its size and even its direction depend on contact.

item.title: How many years does an earthquake cost an economy?
item.description: For most countries, national output recovers within a few years. The places hit hardest can carry the loss for decades.

item.title: Bread on the table, and diabetes
item.description: What the grain has kept matters more than whether bread is eaten at all.

item.title: Does consuming more mean living better?
item.description: Income and life satisfaction rise together, but each step buys less than the one before. The argument is over where, and for whom, it stops.

item.title: How is sea level measured?
item.description: A rise of a few millimetres a year is built from tide gauges, satellites and a correction for land that moves.

item.title: Why are rivers running dry?
item.description: Some of the world's great rivers no longer reach the sea for part of the year. The main cause lies upstream, in fields and reservoirs.

item.title: How do city lights affect sleep?
item.description: Most people now live under a night sky that never fully darkens. The body's clock reads that light as a signal.

item.title: How much water do data centres use?
item.description: The answer has two parts: the water evaporated to cool the servers, and the water used to make their electricity.

item.title: The carbon books, reconciled
item.description: National inventories and satellite measurements are being read against each other – not as a headline, but as an accounting problem.

item.title: Which languages keep the record
item.description: A public figure can be careful and still stop at the border of the language it was released in.

item.title: After ten million
item.description: A megacity used to be an exception. The public record now has enough of them to compare the planning, not the skyline.

item.title: How grain actually moves
item.description: Wheat, maize, and rice cross borders as balance sheets before they cross them as ships.

item.title: The register of trials
item.description: A study that never enters a public register is harder to find, and harder to count.
